What you need:

5.5 lbs of waxy or primarily waxy potatoes (floury (?) sorts tend to fall apart)

4-5 ounces of vinegar (white wine vinegar works, I like balsamic vinegar better for the taste but some people find the dark colour off-putting)

15 ounces of stock (anything except fish stock works)

a table spoon of mustard (the yellow paste, dijon mustard won't work because it won't thicken the dressing properly)

2-3 onions

salt and pepper

herbs (chives, parsley, what ever you like)

4-5 ounces of olive oil (get some good olive oil, it'll end up tasting a lot less greasy than with sunflower or peanut oil)

Here's how you make it: (keep in mind that you'll have to put it aside for a few hours so if you plan on having a BBQ, I'd suggest making the salad around lunch time)

Wash the potatoes (you're going to use the pot again so make sure they're clean).

Add plenty of salt to the cooking water and cook the potatoes until they're almost done, about three quarters in. DON'T finish them or they'll fall apart later-on. Put them in cold water, that'll make them easier to peel.

Set up the stock (use the pan you used for the potatoes, you'll need a big enough bowl anyways).

Add the vinegar and the mustard, whisk until it's homogenous. Don't add the oil yet, it'll separate.

Heat the dressing back up (don't add the herbs yet, they'll go lumpy).

Slice the potatoes into ~1/4 inch thick slices, add them to the dressing.

Cut the onions and mix them in too.

If you shake the pot a bit, the potato slices should be just submerged in broth/vinegar/mustard. Keep in mind that you can always add more later-on if you need.

Keep the pot on the stove plate until the potatoes have heated up again until you can see it steam (that's why you shouldn't cook them through - they'll fall apart now). Just heat it up, DO NOT let it boil.

Pull the pot away, let it cool down. Stir from time to time. As the salad cools down over the next couple of hours, the starch from the potatoes should visibly thicken the dressing, making it nice and creamy. The potatoes should now be fully cooked, too. If it gets too thick, add stock.

Before serving, add the olive oil and herbs. Stir gently. It should look like this now (or the same in brown-ish if you used balsamic vinegar). It's best when it's still slightly warm but room temperature works just fine.

These guys spend most of the time in theater having a roller coaster ride of extreme adrenaline highs and crashes for months. The amount of stress put on someone in that situation is off the charts, constantly having to be acutely aware of your surroundings at all times. The mental and physical exhaustion just from that alone, not to mention the actual physicality of being in a combat situation itself takes a huge toll. Top that with death, disparity, and witnessing/or participant in, temporary or otherwise, loss of morality that war brings, and it's a cocktail of disaster waiting to happen. When their tour is up, they come home and are pretty much dumped back into civilian society cold turkey. There is a few organizations that can help, but most don't use them as the stigma for doing so is not entirely good.

So, when back home, people at home wife, family , friends, (if they have no military background for mutual understanding) just expect them to pick up where they left off before they went over seas. That is the hardest on these guys, because they needs to get used to civilian life slowly. A lot can do it, yes, and that's great because they are better off, but many others can not. They want desperately to seem normal, pick up their life, try to fall in line with expectations at home, causing a whole new stress/pressure on them making things worse. Wife, family and friends, although well meaning, can miss the warning signs of trouble.

Some of the signs are: They start to withdraw, have a hard time holding conversations or relating to civilians/"normal" life, have strong mood swings, become frustrated over small issues, have trouble eating or over eat, wants to be surrounded by military friends, or only wants to talk about the military (because in a lot of cases they have to relearn to be civilians again and people don't give them the time to do so), and the worse sign, chemical dependency legal or illegal. Add on issues from any medical problems from injuries they may have suffered.

As a result, wife/friends get upset because they don't have the person they were when they left, family, same issue, some are against what they did there, are disgusted if they took part in killing people, seeing how the military is treated in media (social and otherwise), family/friends/acquaintances don't know how to act around them or try to over compensate with well meaning behavior/advice that is pressed on them. People start to drift away.

Jobs in the US are also not what they were in the 80's when it was a boon to have military service on your resume. Unless you work for state, federal govt , or business sympathetic to former military, private sector has a very different view of hiring them, especially if they are/were enlisted. They don't trust them, see them as loose cannons, or that they are not reliable, have medical issues, in the end they are seen as a liability and are more readily passed over for positions.

Top all that off with the terrible issues of the VA medical system when they want or need help, and it's a powder keg of issues that military and former military have to go through.
